common_name: Byers Golden Possumhaw Holly (Yellow-Fruited Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Byers Golden is a female selection and needs a male Ilex decidua nearby to set its distinctive yellow fruit.

directions: Byers Golden is a yellow-fruited sport of native possumhaw, dropping its leaves each fall to reveal bare branches studded with clear golden berries rather than the orange-red typical of the species, a striking alternative for gardeners who want the possumhaw winter display in a warmer color. Like all possumhaw selections it is dioecious, so a male seedling or named male clone must grow within range for the female to set fruit, and the berries persist on bare stems well into late winter, feeding mockingbirds, robins, and cedar waxwings after most other food sources are exhausted. It tolerates both moist bottomland soils and drier upland sites once established, making it as adaptable as the species it was selected from. Prune lightly right after the berry display fades if a tidier form is wanted, since flower buds for next year's crop form on new growth soon after.

common_name: Finch's Golden Possumhaw Holly (Gulf Coast Yellow-Fruited Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this female selection needs a male possumhaw growing nearby for reliable fruit set.

directions: Finch's Golden was selected by Gulf Coast horticulturist Bill Finch of Mobile, Alabama, from wild possumhaw populations of the central Gulf South, making it a regionally appropriate choice for zone 8-9 gardens seeking a native alternative to red-berried hollies. Its bare winter branches carry the same heavy fruit set as the species but in clear yellow-gold rather than orange-red, extending the color range of the possumhaw winter display and standing out beautifully against a dark evergreen backdrop. As with all possumhaw, it is dioecious and depends on a male plant within pollinating range for berries, which then persist on the leafless stems into late winter as an important food source for overwintering songbirds. It shares the species' tolerance for both seasonally wet bottomland soil and average garden conditions, needing little care once established.
sources: Mobile Botanical Gardens native plant program notes

common_name: Pink Beauty Possumhaw Viburnum (Heavy-Fruiting Smooth Witherod)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Pink Beauty sets the heaviest, most profuse berry crop of the commonly available possumhaw viburnum cultivars.

directions: Pink Beauty is prized among possumhaw viburnum selections for producing the most abundant, densely packed berry clusters of any widely sold cultivar, opening creamy-white flower cymes in early summer that give way to rounded hemispheres of fruit passing from pink to blue to blackened purple as they ripen. The heavy fruit set makes it an especially valuable songbird feeding station in fall, when migrating and resident birds strip the color-shifting clusters over several weeks. Like other Viburnum nudum selections it tolerates wet, poorly drained soil far better than most flowering shrubs, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and low spots in a partly shaded border. Planting a second, genetically distinct viburnum nearby further improves fruit set and berry abundance.

common_name: Cape Cod Inkberry Holly (Compact Native Evergreen Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cape Cod is one of the older and more compact named inkberry selections, useful where a smaller native evergreen hedge shrub is wanted.

directions: Cape Cod is a compact, densely branched selection of native inkberry holly, holding small, glossy, dark evergreen leaves on a tidy mound that stays considerably smaller than the wild species. Female plants produce inconspicuous spring flowers valuable to native bees, followed by small black berries in fall that persist into winter and are eaten by a variety of songbirds. Inkberry is naturally an understory shrub of pine flatwoods and pocosins, and this cultivar carries that same tolerance for wet, acidic soils and considerable shade, making it a useful broadleaf evergreen for foundation plantings or informal hedges beneath high tree canopy. Established plants need little pruning beyond an occasional light shearing to maintain density near the base.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this naturally occurring yellow-fruited form of spicebush was first documented at the Arnold Arboretum and requires a male Lindera benzoin nearby for fruit set.

directions: This uncommon natural form of native spicebush is identical to the typical species in its aromatic foliage, early-spring yellow flowers, and dense understory habit, differing only in producing translucent orange-yellow rather than bright red berries in fall. It offers a subtler, less commonly seen fruit color for gardeners building a native shade collection, while retaining every ecological benefit of common spicebush: the foliage is the exclusive larval host for spicebush swallowtail and promethea silk moth caterpillars, and the fall berries feed migrating thrushes. Because spicebush is dioecious, only female plants of this form bear fruit, and a male spicebush of any form should be planted within about fifty feet to ensure pollination. Site it in the same moist, humus-rich, shaded woodland conditions favored by the straight species, where few other flowering shrubs perform as well.

common_name: Pearl Bleu Arrowwood Viburnum (Heavy Blue-Fruited Native Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pearl Bleu is valued for an unusually dense, abundant fruit set even though individual berries run smaller than most arrowwood cultivars.

directions: Pearl Bleu was selected specifically for producing an unusually heavy load of small, round, deep-blue berries in fall, packed more densely along the stems than most other arrowwood viburnum selections, creating a striking mass display that draws thrushes, catbirds, and other fruit-eating songbirds. Flat, domed clusters of creamy white flowers open in late spring and attract a wide range of native pollinators before the berry display develops. It cross-pollinates readily with other Viburnum dentatum cultivars, and planting a second selection nearby further improves the already heavy fruit set. Like other arrowwood viburnums it adapts to a wide range of soils, from wet to average garden conditions, and tolerates part shade at a woodland edge as well as full sun.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; upland swampprivet is highly drought-tolerant once established and needs no supplemental irrigation in the Gulf South once roots are settled.

directions: Despite the common name, upland swampprivet is a shrub of dry calcareous glades, woodland edges, and coastal shell middens across the southeastern Gulf South rather than true wetlands, distinguishing it from its wetter-growing relative swamp privet (Forestiera acuminata). Tiny, inconspicuous yellow-green flowers open in mid to late summer, later than most native shrubs, providing a modest late-season nectar source, and are followed in early fall by small, glossy blue-black drupes that birds seek out. Its fine-textured, gray-green foliage and naturally dense, twiggy habit make it useful as an unclipped informal screen or massed planting on dry, alkaline, or rocky sites where many broadleaf shrubs struggle. This species is uncommon in cultivation and best sourced from native plant specialty nurseries rather than general garden centers.
sources: Florida Plant Atlas (University of South Florida)

common_name: Green Magic Inkberry Holly (Compact Black-Fruited Evergreen Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Magic is a Willoway Nurseries introduction selected for a tight, compact habit and glossy foliage that holds its dark color through winter.

directions: Green Magic is a low, wide-spreading inkberry selection with glossy, deep-green evergreen foliage that stays notably tighter and denser than the species without regular shearing. Small black berries develop on female plants in fall and persist into winter, providing food for songbirds through the leanest months, while the dense evergreen structure offers year-round cover for nesting and roosting birds. It shares the species' tolerance for wet, poorly drained soils and considerable shade, both traits inherited from its native habitat in coastal pine flatwoods and pocosins, making it a dependable evergreen substitute for boxwood in shaded, damp foundation plantings. Deer generally avoid it, and little pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward stem is needed to keep its naturally rounded form.

common_name: Maryland Beauty Winterberry Holly (Large Red-Fruited Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Maryland Beauty is a female selection that colors up earlier in fall than many winterberry cultivars and needs a male such as 'Jim Dandy' planted nearby for fruit set.

directions: Maryland Beauty is a heavy-fruiting winterberry selection prized for large, bright red berries that thickly cover the bare stems and color noticeably earlier in the season than many other named winterberry cultivars, extending the fall display. As a deciduous holly, it drops its leaves in autumn to expose the full berry crop against the winter landscape, feeding robins, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds through the cold months. It shares the species' natural tolerance for wet, poorly drained, and seasonally flooded soils, making it an excellent choice for rain gardens, pond margins, and low spots that stay consistently moist. Being dioecious, a male winterberry blooming at the same time, such as 'Jim Dandy', must be planted within range for reliable, heavy fruit set.
